runtimeNotes: One line displayed at a time; choices shown only on final line after typing.

No line breaking, clipping or readability has been measured in Unreal by this content audit.

longestLines.text: A gush of water bursts from under the sink, and a big, broad man slides out on the wave. Wet copper curls. A short auburn beard. A soaked white tank top with a red valve wheel where his heart should be. His arms and legs are copper pipe, green at the joints, patched here and there with silver duct tape. He looks you up and down with deep disappointment.

Next page, ringed with hearts: a tall, gaunt, unsmiling man, black hair to his shoulders and tucked behind his ears, a long moss-and-black coat worn open over a bare chest, little black clovers dotted wrist to brow. 'MALCOLM ASHGROVE. My ghost boyfriend. Died 1847 (consumption + heartbreak). Lives in my closet. Hates sunlight (same).'

You open the bedroom closet. The back wall is velvet-black with mold. It shivers, spores drift up like dark glitter, and a tall, gaunt man unfolds from the plaster: ivory-pale, black hair to his shoulders, a long moss-and-black overcoat hanging open over a bare chest. Little black clovers of mold bloom on him, wrist to brow.

He turns to slide back under the sink and leaves a big puddle on the tiles. You reach past him to shut off the tap, step right in it, and your foot goes out from under you.  He lunges to catch you. For one second there's a cold, wet arm around your waist. Then it's just water, and you sit down hard in the puddle.

The tile remembers things. Don't ask me how. A girl had chicken pox in that tub in 1964 and counted every tile. A man hid an engagement ring in the soap dish in 1979. A girl dyed her hair pink in that sink in 1994. Kool-Aid. Good instincts.

You sit on the floor together, close, with one careful inch of air between your shoulders, and read. 2006: Malcolm is a vampire. 2007: he plays the cello in a band. Later in 2007, he and Mr. Darcy duel over Raven, then agree to share her.

The tile shimmers, and a man steps out of the wall. A very, very large man. Shirtless. From the neck down he IS the wall: glossy hot-pink square tile with crisp white grout lines, flaking into bare skin at the collarbones and wrists.

That cord backfeeds the panel. No transfer switch, Gary's old splices, the lot. It sends power out to the street, so the bloke up the pole fixing the lines gets all of it. And the house goes up like a Christmas tree. With you in it.

You open up the east wall together. He talks you through every drip with a wet finger, very close to your ear, being extremely bossy about it. Every time your wrench gets near the wiring he yells 'WYATT'S! DON'T!' like a lifeguard.

Saturday. The storm hits Heartbreak Lane like it's personal. Water is running down the wall BEHIND the tile, and Tyler is holding the wall up with both hands, every enormous tiled muscle in his back braced. Or trying to.

longestReplies.text: Because somebody loved it. And because I love it. All of it. Including the part that argues.
It's not personal. Everything I own is riding on this flip. If it fails, I lose it all.
It's a health hazard, Malcolm. And a resale problem. Both of those are real.
Don't apologize. That's the most useful thing anyone's said to me all week.
Then let's fix it properly. Not cheap. Whoever buys it gets a real home.
You're not the only guy in this house who's been sweet to me, you know.
A leak that's scared of floods? That's like a fish scared of the sea.
Hal built it to outlast them both. It's going to outlast you too. No.
Honestly? Enough to cover my mortgage and then some. That's the job.
Jealous? It's very quiet. Very low maintenance. Unlike some people.
